summary: معاناة واضحة للنجم البرازيلي
body: معاناة واضحة للنجم البرازيلي قدّم البرازيلي فينيسيوس جونيور، نجم ريال مدريد، أداءً باهتًا جديدًا، في فوز فريقه أمام لايبزيج (4-1)، مساء الأربعاء، على ملعب سانتياجو برنابيو، في الجولة الثالثة من مرحلة الدوري في دوري أبطال أوروبا. وشارك فينيسيوس أساسيًا، لكن المدرب جوزيه مورينيو قرر استبداله في الدقيقة 70 لصالح زميله يان ديوماندي، الذي صنع هدفًا وسجّل آخر في 20 دقيقة فقط. وكتب فينيسيوس عبر حسابه الرسمي على "إنستجرام" بعد المباراة: "أعيش اللحظة، كل شيء يمضي". من جانبها وصحفت صحيفة " ماركا " رسالة فينيسيوس بأنها تمزج بين الاستسلام والإيمان، في ظل تعرضه لانتقادات جماهيرية عنيفة منذ بداية الموسم الحالي بسبب تراجع مستواه، إلى جانب الشكوك التي تحوم حول مكانه في التشكيلة الأساسية بعد إيقافه من قبل رابطة الليجا 4 مباريات. لكن مورينيو لم ينضم إلى المنتقدين، بل دافع عن البرازيلي بقوة، حيث قال المدرب البرتغالي: "قدم فيني مباراة رائعة، وأظهر أداءً تكتيكيًا ممتازًا أفاد مدربه والفريق على حد سواء". وأسهب المدرب في الحديث عن مزايا فينيسيوس التي لم تقتصر على تسجيل الأهداف، قائلاً: "لقد نجح في بناء الهجمات من الجناح الأيسر، وأحكم قبضته على المساحات ببراعة، وكاد أن يسجل هدفًا رائعًا لولا تصدي حارس المرمى لتسديدته القوية". title: James Webb telescope discovers surprising trove of metals around the Milky Way's supermassive black hole
summary: New observations from the James Webb Space Telescope reveal a concentration of heavy metals near the Milky Way's central black hole. The discovery deepens a mystery about why our black hole behaves the way it does.
body: The Milky Way's supermassive black hole is surrounded by a surprising trove of heavy metals, according to new observations by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The metals may offer new clues about how Earth got its share of heavy elements — but it could also make one of the greatest mysteries about our local black hole even harder to solve. In astronomy , metals refer to any element heavier than hydrogen or helium, with common examples including oxygen, carbon, iron or gold. These elements are forged through nuclear fusion in the hearts of stars that are reaching the ends of their lives, before being sprayed into space and incorporated into new generations of stars. Scientists say the material spotted by JWST likely came from supernovas ‪—‬ stellar explosions that blasted the metal into the region around Sagittarius A (Sgr A*), the monster black hole in the middle of our galaxy. The metals, detected as gas, appear to have the same composition as several nearby stars, which suggests both the stars and the gas originated at the same time. body: "هناك غضب كبير في الأهلي" فجرت مباراة الأهلي والقناة، التي أقيمت اليوم الأربعاء، في الدوري الممتاز المصري، موجة غضب كبيرة بين جماهير ومسؤولي القلعة الحمراء. انتزع الأهلي تعادلًا مثيرًا مع القناة (3-3)، مساء اليوم الأربعاء على استاد القاهرة، ضمن منافسات الجولة السابعة من الدوري المصري الممتاز. وكان الأهلي متأخرا بنتيجة 3/2 حتى الدقيقة 90+3 التي شهدت تسجيل المغربي أشرف داري لهدف التعادل. وارتفع رصيد المارد الأحمر إلى النقطة 17، في المركز الثاني بجدول ترتيب الدوري، بفارق 4 نقاط عن بيراميدز المتصدر بالعلامة الكاملة، ونقطة عن الزمالك الثالث، بينما رفع القناة رصيده إلى 8 نقاط، في المركز الـ11. ناقش الموضوعات والأخبار بشكل أعمق في منتديات كووورة وقال الإعلامي إبراهيم عبد الجواد، عبر قناة "أون سبورت"، إن التعادل فجر موجة غضب شديدة داخل النادي الأهلي. وقال: "هناك غضب كبير في الأهلي، وهناك 3 قرارات اتخذت بالفعل بعد التعادل الليلة". وأوضح: "الأهلي يدرس جديا إيقاف مستحقات اللاعبين لحين تحسن النتائج، كما تقرر عقد اجتماع مهم غدا بين اللاعبين من جهة، والمغربي حسين عموتة المدير الفني ومعه وائل جمعة، مدير الكرة من جهة أخرى". وختم: "القرار الثالث الذي علمنا به يتمثل في تجديد الثقة في المدرب الحسين عموتة، والتأكيد على أنه لا مساس به، ومنحه الثقة الكاملة لاستكمال عمله في الفترة المقبلة".

title: Extremely rare Viking Age coin from the reign of 'Olaf the Holy' may have been 'held in the king's own hand'
summary: A massive Viking Age hoard that was discovered in Norway contains a rare silver coin featuring "Olaf the Holy," one of the country's first Christian kings.
body: A rare silver coin minted during the reign of a famous Viking king has been discovered in a massive hoard in Norway that now comprises 5,500 coins and counting. The coin is inscribed with the name of the Norwegian king Olaf Haraldsson, who ruled from 1015 to 1028 and, as St. Olaf or "Olaf the Holy," is considered the national saint of Norway. Fewer than 20 coins minted during Olaf's reign have ever been discovered, and the newfound coin is a "national treasure," according to a statement from the University of Oslo's Museum of Cultural History. "Here we have a coin bearing the king's portrait and a cross, with another cross on the reverse," University of Oslo coin expert Svein Gullbekk said in the statement. "It is a Christianisation coin on a grand scale." Olaf is credited with establishing Christianity in Norway — an early step toward its full conversion about a generation later. title: Lightest known pair of neutron stars proves Einstein right yet again
summary: Einstein's theory of relativity just got put to the test by the lightest binary neutron star system ever discovered.
body: Astronomers have discovered the lightest known pair of neutron stars — two ultradense stellar remnants that circle each other every 2 hours, 22 minutes, veering toward an inevitable collision about 82 million years from now. By timing radio pulses from one of the stars, the researchers detected three subtle effects predicted by Albert Einstein 's general theory of relativity and found that the theory describes the pair's motion to within about 1% — proving the visionary physicist right yet again . The researchers published their findings Sept. 15 in the journal Physical Review Letters . Neutron stars are the collapsed cores of massive stars that exploded as supernovas. Each packs more mass than the sun into a ball roughly 12 miles (20 kilometers) in diameter. Some, called pulsars, spin rapidly and sweep beams of radio waves across the sky like cosmic lighthouses. Their rotation is so steady that their pulses work as extraordinarily precise clocks. Very few pulsars orbit another neutron star. body: Scrubbing Earth of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—a.k.a. PFAS or forever chemicals—could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS have been linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays , cancer , and reduced immune response . They are known for a strong bond between carbon and fluorine, which the environment struggles to break down.  The sticking points PFAS are everywhere: They spew from factories and slough off products and into water with normal use. Scientists have found them in everything from human blood to Antarctic snow . One 2022 report found that 89% of the US population had PFAS in excess of two nanograms per milliliter of blood plasma, a common threshold for potential adverse health effects, and 9% of the population had passed the riskier level of 20 nanograms per milliliter. summary: A gene variant called APOE4 is the biggest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Scientists are finally figuring out how it works.
body: A gene variant called APOE4 dramatically increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer's disease, the most common form of dementia. Now, emerging research is revealing APOE4's true role in the condition, and a new study pinpoints a possible way to treat it. Historically, scientists studying Alzheimer's disease have focused on two proteins that accumulate in patients' brains: amyloid-beta and tau. However, there's a "third thing that people didn't pay attention to, until recently," said study co-author Li-Huei Tsai , a neuroscientist at MIT. That third thing is the accumulation of droplets of fat, or lipids, in the brain, she told Live Science. The APOE gene makes proteins responsible for transporting fat around cells throughout the body and brain. A version of the gene called APOE4, which increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer's three- to 12-fold, makes proteins that are less efficient at this function, Tsai said. But how APOE4 affects different brain cells was not clearly understood. Tsai's team has been working to close that gap for about a decade. title: Black Death had dramatic effect on species diversity as humans abandoned farmland, study finds
summary: Researchers have found that during the Black Death, when a third of Europe's population was wiped out, biodiversity fell. Understanding the farming practices of the time could help us increase diversity in modern agriculture.
body: When millions of people died in Europe during the Black Death, biodiversity suffered too, new research suggests. The findings suggest that human activities once promoted biodiversity in the landscape — and experts say we could use these findings to boost biodiversity in our modern agricultural landscapes. The 14th century was a tumultuous time for the people of Europe. Persistent cold, wet weather at the beginning of the century led to widespread agricultural failures and unprecedented levels of starvation in what became known as the Great Famine from 1315 to 1317. This was followed by the Black Death , an epidemic of bubonic plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis that killed more than a third of Europe's population. As a result of the widespread deaths and resultant social upheaval, large swaths of agricultural land were abandoned. Population levels didn't begin to recover until the 16th century . title: Can cuttlefish hypnotize their prey?
summary: Cuttlefish use rapid color-change while hunting. The question is, does it actually hypnotize their prey?
body: Like their cephalopod cousins the octopuses , cuttlefish are masters of disguise. As they hunt, these marine predators send waves of color across their skin. The rainbow display stops prey in their tracks, granting the cuttlefish just enough time to shoot out two specialized hunting tentacles at lightning speed and snatch them into range of their deadly beaks. But can cuttlefish actually mesmerize prey with their colorful skin changes? Or is something fishier at play? Experts told Live Science that cuttlefish are ingenious hunters, but that there's likely an even more mysterious process than hunter to prey hypnosis going down on the seafloor. A calculated hunter Cuttlefish are visual hunters , using their large, complex eyes to locate and track potential meals. In general, their strategy involves a slow, stealthy approach, said Bret Grasse , the manager of cephalopod operations at the Marine Biological Laboratory in Woods Hole Massachusetts. body: "Necklaces" of ultracold atoms have provided new evidence to support a nearly 100-year-old quantum theory. In 1931, physicists were trying to use quantum mechanics to explain why some materials are magnetic. Then, a young physicist named Hans Bethe looked at a single row of electrons. Each electron's spin can point up or down. body: Some of the first people in North America lived through extreme climate change at the peak of the last ice age, a new study suggests. Researchers studied ancient pollen locked in rocks at White Sands National Park in New Mexico, which houses an archaeological site thought to contain the oldest human footprints in the Americas . The researchers previously dated those footprints to around 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, though their age is the subject of some scientific debate because they are significantly older than other Indigenous sites in the Americas . The new findings, published Wednesday (Oct. 14) in the journal Science Advances , suggest that humans kept using White Sands after temperatures warmed and thus saw the landscape undergo rapid changes during the coldest era of the last ice age, known as the Last Glacial Maximum (26,500 to 19,000 years ago). "It's remarkable that early humans in the region were real-time witnesses to a rapidly changing environment discernible within a human lifetime — that is really food for thought," study co-author Kathleen Springer , a research geologist at the U.S. Geological Survey, said in a statement. title: Physicists claim they can predict when AI will turn dangerous
summary: A new mathematical formula tracks an AI's internal "compass needle" to flag undesirable outputs before they happen.
body: Researchers say they've developed a simple mathematical formula that can predict when certain ChatGPT-like artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots will "go rogue," suddenly switching from helpful responses to potentially harmful ones. In a new study published Oct. 8 in the journal Patterns, physics professor Neil Johnson and doctoral student Frank Yingjie Huo , both at The George Washington University, show how the order in which a chatbot is given certain prompts can drastically reshape its answers, leading to "tipping points" that can send the chatbot down a rabbit hole of bad advice. However, Johnson and Huo say their formula can easily predict these tipping points.There have been horror stories of AI encouraging users into suicide , helping build lethal weapons , and amplifying violent or harmful points of view . body: Archaeologists digging in the medieval city of Great Zimbabwe have discovered pieces of jade-green Chinese pottery, suggesting that the enigmatic empire had long-distance connections with East Asia more than 1,000 years ago. Great Zimbabwe , located in the southeastern part of modern-day Zimbabwe, was the capital of an ancient empire that arose in southeastern Africa in around A.D. 1000. Little is known about this precolonial empire because its people did not leave a written history, but new archaeological excavations are shining a light on the enormous scale of the centuries-old civilization known for its intricate metalworking and ritual stone carvings. title: Flightless Jurassic bird was like a carnivorous pheasant with killer claws
summary: An early bird with many dinosaur-like features discovered in China seems to have been a fast-running, land-based carnivore with killer claws.
body: Illustration of the flightless Jurassic bird Y uezhuornis yangyuanensis , which had features of both birds and dinosaurs. (Image credit: Mr. Chung-Tat Cheung) Paleontologists in China have discovered a small Jurassic bird that was likely a land-based predator — like a carnivorous pheasant with killer claws. It had some features of birds and others of dinosaurs, suggesting that the earliest birds had a greater diversity of lifestyles than previously recognized. Jurassic birds first emerged 150 million to 148 million years ago, and fossils of them are rare, so experts are just starting to understand how early birds diversified and evolved the ability to fly. The researchers discovered the newly identified Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis in 2024, in the fossil assemblage known as the Upper Jurassic Zhenghe Fauna in southeastern China. It lived 150 million to 148 million years ago, roughly when birds started to appear in the fossil record. The team published their findings Wednesday (Oct. 14) in the journal Nature . title: One of America's biggest meteor craters is 100 million years younger than we thought — and coincided with a global extinction event
summary: Analysis of tiny zircon crystals buried within the 10-mile-wide Ames crater in northwest Oklahoma suggests that the submerged structure dates back to 370 million years ago, during the Frasnian-Famennian mass extinction event.
body: One of America's largest meteor craters is around 100 million years younger than scientists thought, which means the ancient impact coincided with — and potentially contributed to — one of the biggest global extinction events in Earth's history, according to a new study. The underground impact structure, known as Ames crater, is located in northern Oklahoma and is named after a small town that sits above the submerged crater. At around 10 miles (16 kilometers) wide, it is the fourth-largest impact structure in the U.S. Ames crater was created when an Eiffel Tower-size space rock slammed into our planet at more than 70,000 mph (110,000 km/h). At the time, the region was covered in a shallow ocean, and the crater was subsequently buried beneath layers of seafloor sediment. Therefore, there are no visible signs of the crater at the surface today. It was only discovered in 1991, when oil prospectors accidentally drilled into it. Until now, researchers thought Ames crater dated to the Ordovician meteor event around 467 million years ago.
